title: Mathematical Operations
summary: Operator-substitution puzzles: signs are redefined or interchanged, equations must be balanced, and the correct equation picked from four. The arithmetic is primary-school level — marks are lost to BODMAS slips and half-applied substitutions, not to difficulty. A disciplined rewrite-then-evaluate habit makes this one of the safest scoring topics in the paper.

subtopics.title: Operator puzzles and BODMAS
subtopics.concept:
These questions play with the *operators* of an arithmetic expression: they swap meanings ('+' means '÷'), swap numbers, or ask which equation is correctly balanced. The arithmetic itself is school-level — the test is **discipline**, not maths.

Two non-negotiables:

1. **Substitute first, calculate second.** Rewrite the expression with the new operators, then compute. Substituting while calculating is where sign slips happen.
2. **BODMAS** — Brackets, Orders, Division/Multiplication (equal rank, left to right), Addition/Subtraction (equal rank, left to right). Almost every wrong option in this topic is a *left-to-right* evaluation of a correctly substituted expression.

Spend two calm seconds writing the substituted line; the rest is arithmetic you cannot get wrong.

formulas.name: BODMAS order
formulas.note: D and M share a rank and resolve left to right; so do A and S.

formulas.name: Substitution map
formulas.note: A bijection: rewrite every operator before touching any number.

tricks.title: Rewrite the whole line, then compute
tricks.body: Under the given expression, write the substituted operators in the same positions. Only then evaluate with BODMAS. One rewritten line prevents every 'multiplied out of habit' error.

example.solution: Substitution on paper, evaluation under it — never simultaneously.

mistakes: Applying the substitution to only some operators (the last one is most often forgotten).
Evaluating strictly left to right when BODMAS is expected — the examiner counts on exactly this.
Reading the mapping backwards: '+' means '÷' means wherever + *appears*, write ÷.

subtopics.title: Sign substitution
subtopics.concept:
The standard format: *'If + means ÷, − means ×, × means +, ÷ means −, then <expression> = ?'* All four operators are reassigned at once. Workflow: write the mapping, rewrite the expression, evaluate with BODMAS.

Know the three planted options in almost every such question:

- the **correct** value (substitution + BODMAS),
- the **original-expression** value (candidate ignored the mapping),
- the **left-to-right** value of the substituted line (candidate skipped BODMAS).

Computing the original value as a cross-check takes ten seconds and tells you which trap is laid out.

tricks.title: Compute the trap values too
tricks.body: After the correct value, evaluate the original expression once. If that number sits among the options, you have confirmed the examiner's design and your own substitution in one stroke.

example.q:
**Q.** If '+' means '÷' and '×' means '+', evaluate 8 + 4 × 2.

**Sol.** Substituted: 8 ÷ 4 + 2 = 2 + 2 = **4**. Original value: 8 + 4×2 = 16 — an 'ignored the mapping' trap.
example.solution: Two evaluations — substituted and original — finish and self-check the question.

mistakes: Changing numbers instead of operators (the mapping speaks only of signs).
Losing track when the same operator appears twice — every occurrence must be replaced.
Forgetting that after substitution the ÷/× may sit where +/− used to, changing the BODMAS order.

subtopics.title: Interchanging signs and numbers
subtopics.concept:
Twin of substitution, but the change is a **symmetric swap**: 'interchange + and ×' (and sometimes two numbers, e.g. 2 and 8). Wherever one symbol stood, the other now stands, and vice versa. Apply every swap in a single rewrite, then BODMAS.

The **fix-the-equation** variant gives a false equation and asks which two numbers (or signs), if interchanged, make it correct. This is a *sweep*, not an insight: try the pairs in a fixed order (say, always from the left), evaluate each rewritten equation in writing, and stop at the pair that balances. With four numbers there are at most six pairs — under a minute of arithmetic, with zero guessing.

tricks.title: Swap table in the margin
tricks.body: Write 'a ↔ b', 'op1 ↔ op2' at the left, rewrite the expression once with all swaps applied, evaluate.

example.q:
**Q.** Interchange + with × and 2 with 6 in 2 + 6 × 3.

**Sol.** After swap: 6 × 2 + 3 = 12 + 3 = **15**.
example.solution: One rewrite covering every swap beats applying them piecemeal.

tricks.title: Fixed-order sweep for fix-the-equation
tricks.body: Sweep pairs left to right: (n1,n2), (n1,n3), (n1,n4), (n2,n3), (n2,n4), (n3,n4). One written value per row; the row matching the RHS is the answer. If no row matches, you mis-evaluated something — redo the row, not the method.

example.solution: Six written trials, always in the same order — mechanical and safe.

mistakes: Swapping the signs but forgetting the numbers (or the reverse) in two-part interchanges.
Swapping numbers that appear more than once without checking every occurrence.
Abandoning the sweep halfway — the correct pair is often the last one you would try.

subtopics.title: Balancing and operator-filling
subtopics.concept:
Three shapes live here:

1. **Pick the correct equation** — four complete equations are offered; exactly one is arithmetically true. Evaluate all four with BODMAS, in writing, and tick the true one. This is the cheapest correct mark in the whole section (four one-line evaluations, ~40 seconds).
2. **Fill the operator blanks** — '5 ? 2 ? 3 = 13' with sign-pair options like (×, +). Test each pair in order; the balancing pair wins.
3. **Choose the sign set** — three blanks, options are full sign sets such as '÷, +, ×'. Same method: evaluate each set, keep the one that matches the RHS.

The examiner plants one option that would be true if evaluated left to right but fails under BODMAS (or vice versa). If your evaluation disagrees with the key, re-check the *order of operations* before re-checking the arithmetic.

tricks.title: Evaluate all, then eliminate
tricks.body: In pick-the-correct-equation, evaluate every option in a written value column. Exactly one row matches its RHS; the column doubles as your final check.

example.solution: A four-row value column settles it; never stop at the first 'plausible' option.

mistakes: Scanning options for a 'nice-looking' equation instead of evaluating.
Testing only the first blank of a sign pair — the second sign is where the balance usually breaks.
Ignoring equal ranks: ÷ then × must be done left to right, not 'multiplication always first'.

pyqPatterns.approach: Rewrite the whole line with new operators, evaluate with BODMAS; expect the original-value trap among the options.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Four complete equations; exactly one is true.
pyqPatterns.approach: Evaluate all four in a written value column; the true one is the answer.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Interchange + and ×' (sometimes also two numbers), then evaluate.
pyqPatterns.approach: One margin rewrite applying all swaps at once, then BODMAS.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Fix the equation by swapping numbers
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A false equation; some pair of numbers makes it true — find the pair.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fixed-order sweep of all pairs with one written value per row.
Evaluate each candidate set with BODMAS until one balances.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Substitution where the expression carries brackets.
pyqPatterns.approach: Substitute first; brackets still resolve first inside BODMAS.

solvedExamples.q: If **+ means ×**, **− means ÷**, **× means +** and **÷ means −**, then the value of **6 + 2 × 4 ÷ 2 − 2** is:
solvedExamples.solution: Substitute: 6 + 2 × 4 ÷ 2 − 2 → **6 × 2 + 4 − 2 ÷ 2**. BODMAS: 6×2 = 12; 2÷2 = 1; 12 + 4 − 1 = **15**. The option 8 is the original expression's value 6 + 8÷2 − 2 (mapping ignored), and 7 is the left-to-right value of the substituted line (BODMAS skipped).
solvedExamples.shortcut: Rewrite the full line once with new operators, then BODMAS — never substitute while calculating.

solvedExamples.q: If the signs **+ and × are interchanged**, then the value of **3 × 4 + 5 − 6** is:
solvedExamples.solution: Swapping + and ×: 3 × 4 + 5 − 6 → **3 + 4 × 5 − 6**. BODMAS: 4×5 = 20; 3 + 20 − 6 = **17**. (11 is the unswapped value; 29 is what you get if you work strictly left to right: (3+4)×5−6.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: Rewrite with the swapped signs, then multiply first — the swap changes which operator the BODMAS rank picks up.

solvedExamples.q:
Which two numbers should be interchanged to make the following equation correct?

**4 + 2 × 6 − 3 = 20**
solvedExamples.shortcut: Fixed-order sweep of all six pairs, one written value per row; only one row can match the RHS.
solvedExamples.pattern: fix the equation by swapping numbers

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following equations is **correct**?
solvedExamples.shortcut: A written value column for all four options — the true equation is the only row matching its RHS.

practice.q: If **+ means ×** and **× means −**, then the value of **3 + 4 × 2** is:
practice.solution: Substituted: 3 × 4 − 2 = 12 − 2 = **10**. (11 is the original expression's value 3 + 4×2; 14 comes from (3+4)×2 — reading the original left to right.)
practice.shortcut: Two operators swapped: rewrite, then multiply before subtracting.

practice.q: If **÷ means +**, **+ means −**, **× means ÷** and **− means ×**, then the value of **16 ÷ 4 + 3 × 6 − 2** is:
practice.solution: Substituted: 16 ÷ 4 + 3 × 6 − 2 → **16 + 4 − 3 ÷ 6 × 2**. BODMAS: 3÷6×2 = 1 (left to right); 16 + 4 − 1 = **19**. The value 20 belongs to the un-substituted expression (4 + 18 − 2) — the mapping-ignored trap.
practice.shortcut: Rewrite all four operators first; handle the ÷/× run (3 ÷ 6 × 2) left to right.

practice.q: If the signs **+ and ×** and the numbers **2 and 8** are interchanged, then the value of **2 + 8 × 3 − 5** is:
practice.solution: Apply both swaps in one rewrite: 2 + 8 × 3 − 5 → **8 × 2 + 3 − 5** = 16 + 3 − 5 = **14**. (21 is the value with no interchange at all: 2 + 24 − 5.)
practice.shortcut: One rewrite carrying both swaps; then multiply before adding.

practice.q: Which set of signs will make **12 ? 4 ? 2 = 6** correct?
practice.shortcut: The ÷/× pair works rank-to-rank left to right: 12 ÷ 4 × 2 — divide first, then multiply.

practice.q: Which pair of signs will make **5 ? 2 ? 3 = 13** correct?
practice.shortcut: Under BODMAS the second sign's rank decides: × then + multiplies first (2×3? no — 5×2 first).

practice.q: Which of the following equations is **arithmetically correct**?
practice.shortcut: Four one-line evaluations; note 36 ÷ 6 × 2 must go left to right (12), not ×-first (3).

practice.q: If **+ means ÷**, **− means ×** and **÷ means +**, then the value of **(24 + 8) − 2 ÷ 4** is:
practice.solution: Substitute (brackets still first): (24 + 8) − 2 ÷ 4 → (24 ÷ 8) × 2 + 4 = 3 × 2 + 4 = **10**. The un-substituted value is (32 × 2) ÷ 4 = 16 — the mapping-ignored trap.
practice.shortcut: Resolve the bracket with its NEW operator, then sweep the rest by BODMAS.

practice.q: If the signs **+ and − are interchanged**, in which of the following equations does the equation become **correct**?
practice.solution: Swap + and − in each option, then evaluate: 10 + 4 − 2×3 = 14 − 6 = **8** ✓. The others give 12 − 3 + 3 = 12 ✗; 9 − 6 + 12 = 15 ✗; 15 + 5 − 8 = 12 ✗.
practice.shortcut: Interchange first, evaluate second — the RHS is untouched by a sign swap.

practice.q: If **− means +** and **+ means −**, then the value of **15 − 7 + 4 + 2** is:
practice.solution: Substituted: 15 − 7 + 4 + 2 → **15 + 7 − 4 − 2** = 22 − 6 = **16**. (14 is the original line's value 15 − 7 + 4 + 2.)
practice.shortcut: Only +/− swap: pure left-to-right addition-subtraction after the rewrite.

practice.q:
Which two numbers should be interchanged to make the following equation correct?

**8 × 4 − 6 + 3 = 35**
practice.shortcut: Try the pair touching the last operator early — (6,3) — then confirm no earlier pair matched.
practice.pattern: fix the equation by swapping numbers

practice.q: If **÷ means +**, **− means ÷**, **× means −** and **+ means ×**, then the value of **18 ÷ 6 − 3 × 2 + 4** is:
practice.solution: Substituted: 18 ÷ 6 − 3 × 2 + 4 → **18 + 6 ÷ 3 − 2 × 4**. BODMAS: 6÷3 = 2 and 2×4 = 8; 18 + 2 − 8 = **12**. (24 is the left-to-right value; 1 is the original expression's value 3 − 6 + 4.)
practice.shortcut: Rewrite, then clear both ÷/× blocks before touching +/−.

practice.q: If the signs **× and ÷ are interchanged**, then the value of **36 ÷ 4 × 3 − 5** is:
practice.shortcut: ×/÷ swaps keep the same BODMAS rank — just read the rewritten line left to right within the rank.

practice.q: Which set of signs will make **24 ? 8 ? 4 ? 2 = 11** correct?
practice.shortcut: Clear the ÷/× rank first in every candidate: 24÷8 = 3 and 4×2 = 8, then combine.

practice.q: If **+ means ×** and **× means −**, then the value of **(16 + 8) × 2 − 6** is:
practice.shortcut: Bracket first with the NEW operator, then a plain left-to-right −/− sweep.

practice.q: If **'+' means '÷'** and **'−' means '×'**, then the value of **20 + 5 − 2** is:
practice.solution: Substituted: 20 + 5 − 2 → 20 ÷ 5 × 2. Same BODMAS rank, so left to right: 4 × 2 = **8**. (30 is the original value 20 + 10; 50 is (20 + 5) × 2.)
practice.shortcut: After substitution, ÷ and × are equal-rank: 20 ÷ 5 × 2 must go strictly left to right.
